title: The More Digital Selling Gets, the More Human It Needs to Be: A Conversation with Morgan Ingram
body_markdown:
There was a point in my recent conversation with Morgan Ingram, founder of AMP Social, where I realized we were talking about something bigger than sales tactics. We were actually talking about trust.


Morgan has spent his career close to the frontlines of selling—from SDR to sales leader to now running AMP Social—and he has a pretty strong conviction about where things are headed.


His POV? As more of the internet becomes automated, sales is going to have to become more human. To be clear: more human does not equal less digital. Let's break down what that means in this article.


If you want to watch the full episode of the Sales Operator Series featuring Morgan,[check it out here](https://youtu.be/YEGVecR2TGA?si=74jnwc1FjUVzv0Jg) .


## We've Optimized the Relationship Out of Selling


Over the last decade or so, we've gotten really good at turning sales into a process. Cadences, sequences, automated follow-ups, CRM stages, activity targets, mass personalized emails, and so on and so on.


None of those things are inherently bad, and many of them have solved real problems by making sales more repeatable and giving organizations a way to operate at scale.


But somewhere along the way, the machinations started taking over and the relationships started getting lost.


Morgan described it well: Wen every interaction is designed around moving someone to the next stage, the experience becomes transactional—and the buyer can feel it. As a buyer, it might look like:


You have a second conversation with a seller and suddenly they're asking who the financial decision-maker is.


Or maybe you get a LinkedIn message that references a post you made six months ago.


Your inbox is full of emails that are technically personalized but somehow all sound exactly the same as the next.


In all of these instances, the seller is probably following the process perfectly... but the buyer feels zero trust or thoughtfulness.


## The Next Advantage May Be Getting Off the Internet


Morgan has a snazzy framework for how he thinks salespeople need to operate going forward. It goes like this: URL, IRL, catch them all. Let's go through each phase.


URL is the digital world, which is often the place where you first get someone's attention. Likely that's going to be LinkedIn, email, or a page on your website.


IRL is in real life. Meeting someone at a conference or tradeshow, or taking a prospect out to dinner or a round of golf.


And "catch them all" means collecting the most valuable piece of information you can have in a world where digital communication is increasingly noisy: someone's actual phone number.


If you're thinking this framework sounds almost like a return to an older version of sales, that's the point.


Like other revenue leaders I've interviewed for this series, Morgan believes we're heading toward a world where digital channels become so saturated with AI-generated content and automated interactions that getting someone's attention (and more importantly, earning their trust) will require more time in the real world.


His prediction is that we'll even see "field SDRs" again: people whose job isn't just to sit behind a laptop and run sequences, but to get into the markets where their buyers actually live.


A few years ago, at the height of the sales process automation frenzy, that would have sounded crazy to me (and probably to a lot of other folks in this industry). But now, I'm starting to see how we'll start to come full circle and end up back in slightly slower, far more human sales cycle.


## The Goal More Relationships, Not Just More Meetings


To be super clear: the shift Morgan's describing isn't necessarily about replacing outbound with events—at least, not completely. It's more about changing what happens after you get someone's attention.


Rather than treating every prospect like a transaction to be advanced through a funnel, treat them like a relationship worth investing in.


Morgan gave a great example from his work with AppZen.


One of their top reps, Michael, decided to build a more intentional in-person strategy around his accounts. The results went well beyond a few nice conversations. When he shifted to a more IRL process, he:


- Closed a $74,000 deal
- Turned another deal from red to green
- Generated Fortune 500 pipeline
- Built a VIP referral program


Because he spent time with customers and prospects in person, he learned more, built trust, and created opportunities that probably wouldn't have appeared out of a sales sequence.


## Trust Is Built When You Stop Trying to Look Perfect


That brings us to another part of Morgan's philosophy that I think belongs in this conversation. He believes trust is the most important currency we have in sales.


And one of the easiest ways to build it is to be honest when things *don't* work.


He told a story about being asked on a podcast whether a strategy he'd been promoting had worked. The truth was it hadn't. In fact, it had gone terribly. Unlike many folks, his first instinct wasn't to spin the result or pretend he'd learned some brilliant lesson from it. He just said so.


He gave another example of realizing he'd delivered a poor session for a client. Instead of glossing over it, he started the next conversation by telling the team that he felt like he'd wasted their time and had come prepared to make it right.


That kind of transparency can feel almost radical in a world where everyone is publishing their wins and spinning everything into a success story.


But it makes sense that this approach stands out. If everyone can manufacture polished content, polished communication becomes less meaningful.


## We're Going to Have to Learn How to Sell Differently


Digital selling isn't disappearing. But Morgan predicts that the balance will change. Of course salespeople will still use LinkedIn, send emails, and make cold calls. They'll also spend more time in the field, hosting dinners and local events, and building communities. Those are all important ways of turning digital relationships into real ones.


We've spent years making sales more scalable, but we're entering a period where everyone has access to the same tools for scaling.


AI is making research faster, content cheaper, and outreach easier. When everything is steadily becoming more abundant, the things that are harder to manufacture—like trust, judgment, and relationships—become more valuable.


The future of sales may look surprisingly old-fashioned. And in a world increasingly filled with machines trying to get our attention, that might be exactly what makes it work.


Big thanks to Morgan for sharing a great conversation. If you enjoyed this recap, you can find our full interview, as well as other episodes of the Sales Operator Series,[here on Youtube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCigm_W9bMgscGAAl5C3U7ZnwYIMw2Lu3) .
